Chapter 24

Writes: command and form

Commands with single-flight refreshes, a publish form that works with JavaScript off, invalid(issue.handle(...)) for a 409 under the right field, two submit buttons, a redirect from a form handler, a per-card delete form with remove.for(id), and what the browser is handed when a write is refused.

By the end of this chapter

Choose between command and form, refresh exactly the queries a write changed in the same response, and turn a server error into a field message.

Two kinds of write. A command is a function the browser calls from JavaScript — a play was heard, a heart was pressed. A form is a <form>: it posts, it works with JavaScript off, and with enhance it is taken over without a reload. Publishing is a form because it is the one write that should survive a broken script.

Commands, and what they refresh

requested(getCounts, 8).refreshAll() is the server half of an optimistic update. The browser called recordPlay(id).updates(getCounts(id).withOverride(...)) — bump the number on screen now, and *name* the query it wants refreshed. requested refreshes exactly the instances the client named, up to eight, and the real counts come back in the same response as the command’s result. One round trip, no stale number. And in SvelteKit 3 it is not optional: a refresh the client asked for and the server did not answer fails that query on the *client*, once the response is back, with a 400 HttpError, “Requested update was not handled by the remote function”. The server did nothing wrong by its own lights; the browser notices that the key it asked for is missing from the answer. So every command or form that a caller drives with .updates(…) either refreshes what was named — requested(…).refreshAll() here, getMine().refresh() in remove — or says ignore() on purpose.

void getPattern(id).refresh() is the other kind of refresh: server-driven. This handler *knows* getPattern(id) changed, so it says so, and any browser with that query open gets the new value in the response — whether or not it asked. The two compose: the client names what it is showing, the server names what it changed.

The publish form

The schema *is* the form: publish.fields.handle and the rest in the studio (ch. 20) are typed from it. The pattern travels as one hidden field of JSON named _pattern. The underscore is SvelteKit’s convention for a value that must not be echoed back into the page after a failed non-JS submission — designed for passwords, and just as useful for two kilobytes the studio already holds.

Why invalid(issue.handle(...))

claimHandle says “taken” with a 409, which on a page would be an error page. On a form it should be a message under the handle field. issue.handle(message) builds that issue, and invalid(...) throws it so that the form re-renders with the message in publish.fields.handle.issues() — and, with JavaScript off, with the other fields still filled in. A plain invalid("...") with no field is a form-level issue, shown by allIssues(); the unreadable-pattern case uses that, because no field a person typed is at fault.

Two submit buttons share the form and action says which was pressed. For “open”, the handler throws redirect(303, resolve("/(app)/p/[id]", { id })) and the enhanced submission follows it to the new pattern’s page; for “stay”, it returns the vanity address and the panel shows it. A redirect from a remote form handler is a remote-functions feature and worked before SvelteKit 3 — the 3.0 release note about enhanced forms that navigate is about use:enhance form *actions* whose action points at another page, which this project does not have. The address is resolve()d rather than written as a string for the same reason as every link (ch. 27): the route id is checked at build time.

The slug loop: boom-bap, then boom-bap-2. Two publishes of the same title in quick succession could both pass the check and meet the unique index (ch. 21); the catch retries with the next number rather than surfacing a 500 for something that is not the person’s fault.

Deleting is a form too, rendered once per card as {...remove.for(id)} in the gallery (ch. 30), so each card has its own pending state. requireArtist() is the authorisation, and the store’s WHERE id = ? AND artist_id = ? is the check that a person deletes only their own.

Choosing and forgetting a handle

Both set a cookie, so both are forms. becomeArtist refreshes whoAmI() — the query the header reads — so the name appears at the top of the page without a reload. And when the form was submitted from a jam room, it calls watchRoom(room).reconnect(): the room’s live stream read the cookie when it opened and still thinks this browser is “someone”; reconnect ends that stream and starts a fresh one, carried back in the same response, and the new one reads the new cookie. The documented case for reconnect is exactly a mutation that changes something a live query depends on.

When a write is refused, in the browser

Everything above is the server’s half: error(404, "Not yours, or not there"), a 409 turned into a field message. The browser’s half is a catch. When a command or an enhanced form submission is refused outright, the promise the page awaited rejects — and what it rejects *with* decides whether the person reads the server’s sentence or a guess.

Why a helper for one line

Because the obvious line is wrong twice over. The rejection is SvelteKit’s HttpError, { status, body }, where body is the App.Error that handleError produced — so the server’s words are body.message. It is not an Error, so (e as Error).message is undefined: the jam room (ch. 31) showed an empty toast for every refused edit. And a catch that ignores the value and prints its own sentence throws away the one thing the server took the trouble to say — which is what the gallery’s “Could not delete that” and the studio’s “Publishing failed” did, before both became the fallback rather than the message. isHttpError tells a refusal from a request that never arrived, which is the only case that gets the caller’s fallback. A failed snippet is the opposite case and must *not* call this: a boundary is handed the App.Error itself, and error.message is already the sentence (ch. 30, 31). One more field is worth carrying: an unexpected failure has the id that handleError logged it under (ch. 26). The error page prints it as a reference; a toast is all somebody sees when a command fails, so messageOf puts it in brackets after the sentence — “Something went wrong on our side. (ref 3f1c…)” — and the person has something to quote. errors.spec.ts pins all three cases.

The server side of this project already read the right field. isHttpError(e) && e.status === 409 and e.body.message in publish and becomeArtist are inside remote functions, where claimHandle throws the HttpError that error(409, …) makes. Only the browser’s reads were wrong, and only a browser showed it: a probe that made each remote function throw, and recorded what every catch and failed snippet was handed.

Checkpoint

  • You can say why publishing is a form and loving is a command.
  • You can explain the difference between requested(...).refreshAll() and getPattern(id).refresh().
  • You can turn a thrown HTTP error into a message under a specific field.
  • You can say what a catch around await lovePattern(id) is handed, and where its message is.
